title: Western Arrernte man's journey of healing after problems with alcohol
content:
Western Arrernte man Tim McNamara yarns about alcohol problems, encouraging others to change
Hermannsburg/Ntaria traditional owner Tim Tjupurrula McNamara describes himself as "a leader, a cultural man and storyteller".
The proud Western Arrernte man is a mentor to boys and men in his community.
He passes on traditional knowledge and builds relationships through activities such as making spears and boomerangs, working with the Hidden Valley Camp Community Centre, the Tangentyere Men's Behaviour Change Program and other groups.
"I am the good leader of the community, good leader of my families," he said.
But Mr McNamara says he has been on a journey to become the man he is.
"Before, I was just nothing. I was just nobody," he said.
Taking ownership
About 10 years ago, Mr McNamara was ordered by a court to attend the Central Australian Aboriginal Alcohol Programs Unit (CAAAPU), a drug and alcohol support service in Alice Springs.
"I was really struggling with my life," he said.
"I got into trouble so many times, drink and drive, domestic violence, and all sorts of things that were related to alcohol."
Mr McNamara completed his mandated program and returned to his community, but says friends and family again tempted him back down the "wrong roads", so he decided to return to the rehabilitation program, this time of his own volition.
"It was my choice to change," he said.
"CAAAPU was the place we was healed from the things that we do … I learned more about what I need in my life."
Sharing the message
Since then, Mr McNamara said he had been on a journey towards accountability and ownership of his own life, describing it as "freedom".
"Freedom means that you are men in charge for everything that you needed not to take the wrong choice," he said.
"I have more freedom and more space and more sharing, stories, connection about countries, the knowledge that you use and pass it on to others, especially the little people, for my grandchildren.
"We need to continue to do these things, as a man, as an Aboriginal man."
Mr McNamara returned to CAAAPU to share his story with other men and show them change is possible.
"My journey takes me quite a while, but it's more to learn and more to teach others to be men, to understand each other, what is our responsibility," he said.
Positive examples 'a catalyst for change'
CAAAPU chief executive Demian Coates said it was "wonderful" to see Mr McNamara sharing his story.
He said while there was a lot of focus on issues such as substance abuse, domestic violence, crime and health gaps in Indigenous communities, there were "literally thousands" of examples of people overcoming and tackling these challenges.
"It's good to hear the other side, where people have been at rock bottom, and they've changed their whole life," he said.
"It's an inspiration. It's a catalyst for change."

title: 4 Indian places where water shapes everyday life
content:
India’s diverse landscape is home to settlements where water is much more than a scenic backdrop. For some communities, lakes and rivers are roads, workplaces and sources of food; for others, homes and agricultural spaces have evolved around constantly changing water levels.
From Manipur’s floating phumdis to Kashmir’s lake settlements and Assam’s river islands, these places offer a glimpse into lifestyles shaped by water.
If one landscape in India most closely resembles a floating world, it is Loktak Lake in Manipur. The lake is known for phumdis — floating masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter that have accumulated over time. Fishing communities have traditionally used these waters for their livelihoods, with small huts and boats scattered across parts of the lake.
Loktak is also home to Keibul Lamjao National Park, the world’s only floating national park. The protected area sits on the lake’s phumdis and is famous for the endangered sangai, or Manipur brow-antlered deer.
Srinagar’s Dal Lake is best known for its houseboats and shikaras, but the lake is also closely intertwined with the lives of communities that live and work on and around its waters. Floating gardens grow vegetables, and boats transport the produce to markets. Early-morning vegetable markets on the lake are among the most distinctive experiences for visitors.
Houseboats, shikaras, fishing and water-based cultivation have together created a way of life that is difficult to separate from the lake itself.
Majuli is technically a river island rather than a floating village, but its existence is deeply tied to the Brahmaputra. Located in Assam, the island has long been home to communities whose lives have adapted to the river’s seasonal flooding, erosion and shifting channels. Agriculture, fishing and boat transport remain important parts of life.
The island is also an important centre of Assamese Vaishnavite culture, with its Satras and traditions of mask-making, music and performing arts.
In the Sundarbans, villages exist within one of the world’s largest mangrove delta systems, where rivers, creeks and tidal channels dominate the landscape. It isn’t a floating village in the literal sense. Instead, it shows communities adapting to a landscape where the boundary between land and water is constantly shifting.
Boats are an important means of transport in many parts of the region, while fishing, crab collection, honey gathering and agriculture support local communities. Life here is also shaped by the challenges of living in a tidal landscape. Cyclones, flooding, erosion and increasing salinity can affect homes and livelihoods.

title: Pearce ready to carve place in AFL history with Freo
content:
Fremantle captain and Tasmanian export Alex Pearce leads team into AFL grand final
In short:
Tasmanian footballer Alex Pearce can create history on Saturday by becoming the Fremantle Football Club's first-ever AFL premiership captain.
Pearce was born and raised on Tasmania's north-west coast, where resilience is bred, and sport reigns supreme.
What's next?
On Saturday, Fremantle face the Brisbane Lions, who are chasing a three-peat, having won the previous two years in a row.
If Fremantle wins the AFL premiership, the year 1995 will not only be known as the year the Dockers entered the AFL.
It'll be known as the birth year of the club's first-ever premiership captain.
Ruth Forrest was not only there on June 9, 1995, at the North West Regional Hospital in Burnie — she was the midwife who delivered Alex Pearce into the world.
"He was a beautiful, big baby," she says.
"And when you hold these babies in your hand after they're born, there's just this unlimited potential in every child."
Thirty-one years later, Pearce stands on the doorstep of football immortality.
Ms Forrest, who Tasmanians know as the independent member for Murchison in the state's upper house, has kept tabs on Pearce since he was a newborn.
"He's just this genuine, inspirational leader. That's what he is," she said.
"To see him grow up into that, it must be huge pride for his family, and I share a tiny bit of that."
Young Alex wanted to play cricket at the MCG
Forrest may have delivered Pearce, but it was parents Scott and Karen who raised him on the coast, in the cradle of Tasmanian sport.
Mum and sister Georgia were star equestrian riders, while Dad was a gun cricketer for Ulverstone.
He still umpires and administers the regional competition, while Uncle Jason remains as president of the Ulverstone Cricket Club.
For young Alex, cricket was the great constant.
"I played my last game of cricket ever with Alex, in a second grade grand final," Scott said.
But footy was in the blood too.
Grandfather Wayne Pearce was a goal machine for the Ulverstone Robins in the 1960s.
"As a kid growing up, his main aim was to play in a Boxing Day Test at the MCG in cricket,"Scott said.
"It's funny how things work out. He's now going to play at the MCG in a grand final as captain of an AFL team, so he got there in the end."
Scott still has to remind himself that his son is indeed on the brink of becoming an AFL premiership captain — a title he never thought Alex would hold.
"Christ, no," he said.
"We knew he had some ability as a junior; he had a growth spurt, played one year with the Tassie Mariners. He didn't play too bad."
"But he wasn't a stand-out player. He was okay," he said.
Out of nowhere, Pearce, who stands 200 centimetres, was drafted to the Dockers at pick 37 in 2013.
From there, he flourished, and the traits that would see him named Dockers captain began to blossom — loyalty, justice and trademark north-west coast resilience that was tested when he fractured his leg twice and didn't play for almost two years.
He forged a connection with a number of Fremantle's First Nations players and began to explore and celebrate his own identity as a Palawa man.
It's a pursuit that his dad is particularly proud of, and that inspired him to delve into his own ancestry.
"It's something I need to do more of, but I'm glad that I've looked into a little bit of it so far," he said.
"As a rule, you didn't look too much into that in years gone by, when I was a kid and in early adulthood.
"But we're very proud of the way he represents the Indigenous people of Tasmania, and it's something he's very proud of as well"
Ulverstone painting the town purple
Then came the confidence, and the individuality.
During COVID, Pearce decided to grow his hair out and pierce his own nose.
Scott said he "doesn't care much about that stuff" — but that he took the news of the piercing "better than his mother did".
Scott's job requires him to be on the road, hopping between Ulverstone, Devonport and Burnie.
His shifts run a little longer, due to locals bailing him up to talk footy, cricket and Alex.
It's indicative of a region where town rivalries are put aside when a coastal son or daughter succeeds.
"We're a footy family and we know Alex personally," Kim Smith, owner of Urban Surf and Co in Ulverstone, said.
"When they won the other night, his mum said to paint the town purple, so we thought why not."
Local real estate agent Jakub Lehman is on board too.
"That's what small communities are there for," he said.
The entire coast is aware of the history that Pearce stands to create if the Dockers defeat Brisbane.
He'd become the third-ever Tasmanian premiership captain, behind the iconic Darrel Baldock and Royce Hart.
And he'd also become the first-ever First Nations-identifying premiership captain.
But to his family, he will still just be Alex — or "Moose".
"That's probably one of the great traits," his dad said.
"He hasn't changed. He hasn't got ahead of himself or anything like that"
"He's just a boy from Ulverstone."

title: I ranger aborigeni che stanno ripulendo le coste australiane dalle reti da pesca fantasma
content:
Le spiagge nordoccidentali dell’Australia sono sempre più invase da reti da pesca abbandonate. Le popolazioni aborigene locali si sono organizzate per fare pulizia.


Le popolazioni indigene dell’Australia stanno ripulendo le spiagge da reti da pesca fantasma. Queste intrappolano specie animali come tartarughe e squali, raccolgono rifiuti in acqua trasportandoli fino a riva e una volta qui si sgretolano in microplastiche che restano nell’ambiente per secoli.
Di fronte a questa emergenza, le comunità indigene si stanno organizzando con apposite squadre di ranger che setacciano centinaia di chilometri di costa e ripuliscono l’ambiente. Un lavoro lungo e faticoso, fatto anche con il supporto di strumenti tecnologici come i droni, e che ha assunto una portata internazionale con il coinvolgimento di altri paesi, come l’Indonesia, per prevenire l’abbandono delle reti da pesca.
Reti da pesca e altri rifiuti
Sulle spiagge dell’Australia si stanno accumulando reti da pesca fantasma. Non sono state abbandonate dai pescatori locali, anche perché vengono rinvenute soprattutto in aree protette della Terra di Arnhem o dell’isola di Groote Eylandt, dove l’accesso è riservato esclusivamente alle popolazioni aborigene, che hanno un rispetto di tipo sacro per la loro terra. Provengono piuttosto dal sud-est asiatico, dove vengono abbandonate in mare dai pescatori e trascinate dalle correnti fino alla costa nord-occidentale australiana.


L’Australia ha un grosso problema di rifiuti lungo le proprie spiagge. La situazione più drammatica è quella delle isole e secondo uno studio pubblicato sulla rivista scientifica Nature, solo sulle isole Cocos nel 2019 sono stati rinvenuti un milione di scarpe, 370 mila spazzolini da denti, 414 milioni di oggetti di plastica per un totale di 238 tonnellate di rifiuti. Negli ultimi anni la situazione è migliorata tanto che una ricerca del 2025 dell’agenzia scientifica nazionale australiana ha certificato una riduzione di un terzo dell’inquinamento lungo le sue coste.
Le problematiche rimangono e quello delle reti da pesca è una delle urgenze del presente. In alcuni casi vengono rinvenute come blocchi di plastica dura dopo che qualcuno ha provato a farle sparire bruciandole e fondendole in blocchi. Una volta sulla spiaggia queste reti si sgretolano in microplastiche che impiegano anche secoli per decomporsi. In altri casi intrappolano rifiuti e specie animali marine che vengono poi trascinati fino a riva, sconvolgendo gli ecosistemi e incrementando l’inquinamento.
La missione dei ranger indigeni
La pulizia delle spiagge nordoccidentali dell’Australia dalle reti da pesca fantasma è diventata un’attività sempre più diffusa tra le popolazioni aborigene locali. Squadre di veri e propri ranger ambientali setacciano tratti di costa che si estendono per centinaia di chilometri servendosi di strumentazione di vario tipo. In mare si muovono chiatte con verricelli che individuano le reti da pesca impigliate sui fondali e che vengono così issate in superficie. In cielo invece volano i droni dotati di intelligenza artificiale che individuano le reti dall’alto.
I ranger del popolo aborigeno Anindilyakwa hanno iniziato a lavorare in collaborazione con la Charles Darwin University e l’utilizzo dei droni ha notevolmente semplificato il loro lavoro, visto che è quadruplicato il numero di reti da pesca fantasma individuate. I ranger del popolo Yolŋu, nella penisola di Gove, nel 2025 hanno rimosso circa 13 tonnellate di detriti marini, tra cui numerose reti da pesca.
Raccolta fondi e cooperazione
Nei punti più inquinati delle coste australiane si contano una media di tre tonnellate di detriti per chilometro. E uno dei problemi, quando si trovano le reti da pesca, è cosa farne. Lo spazio nei depositi e nelle discariche è ormai finito e anche quando si trova un buco succede spesso che i gestori le rifiutino per il timore che possano contenere materiali tossici come il piombo. In alcuni casi le reti vengono donate ad artisti locali che le usano per i loro lavori di tessitura ma l’offerta è di gran lunga superiore alla domanda.
A fine 2025 il governo australiano è intervenuto per dare una mano. Sono stati stanziati 25 milioni di dollari per comprare la strumentazione necessaria per pulire le spiagge e sono stati creati nuovi spazi per lo stoccaggio. Una parte dei fondi è stata invece destinata alla prevenzione, coinvolgendo i paesi del sud-est asiatico responsabili dell’abbandono nelle reti da pesca in campagne di sensibilizzazione destinate ai loro pescatori e in sistemi di monitoraggio efficaci. L’obiettivo del governo australiano e delle popolazioni aborigene delle coste nordoccidentali è quello di eliminare completamente le reti fantasma provenienti da fonti internazionali entro il 2030.

title: Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
content:
National
Nepal tunnel survivor finds solace in village homecoming
Rescued after nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel, Sanjay Sah returned to his family in a village still mourning workers missing after last month’s disaster.Reuters
After nine days trapped in a hydropower tunnel and a week of hospital care following his dramatic rescue, Sanjay Sah, a rare survivor of last month’s devastating glacier collapse in Nepal, finally returned to his village and family on Sunday.
It was a homecoming marked by relief and joy but also grief.
“I was trapped in the tunnel ... I felt trapped in the hospital room too. I finally feel free here in my village,” Sah, 30, said after arriving in Tilathi Koiladi, near the border with India.
At least 1,386 people have died and 5,130 are still missing across Nepal weeks after a Himalayan glacier collapsed near the Chinese border, unleashing a wall of mud and water that crashed through mountain valleys destroying everything in its path.
Around 900 power station workers remain missing. Sah, a mechanical foreman at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, was one of just three pulled from debris-buried tunnels extending deep under the mountains.
He survived in the darkness, drinking flood water and seepage from the mountain rock until rescue workers finally reached him.
Sah left the hospital in the capital Kathmandu on Friday and the next day boarded a bus for an overnight journey home.
A tearful homecoming to a village still in mourning
Around 60 people, mostly women, awaited his arrival in Tilathi Koiladi on Sunday.
Family members, including his parents, uncle, wife and daughter, performed a traditional welcome ceremony, washing his feet as part of a cleansing ritual.
After his mother dabbed a pink vermilion tika on his forehead, Sah bowed. They embraced and then broke down in tears.
“My son!” his mother cried, holding him tightly and kissing him on the cheek.
Women who had gathered to witness the reunion used their colourful saris to wipe the tears from their eyes.
Many in Tilathi Koiladi are still awaiting word of the fate of family members who had been working at hydropower stations hit by the flooding.
“There are more people from my village still missing after the flood,” Sah told Reuters.
One family, he said, phoned him while he was still in the hospital to ask if he had seen or heard from a missing relative who had been working at a different power station. He had to tell them he had not.
At home among family, Sah said he is ready to put his ordeal behind him.
“I will stay in my village for some time now. I want to meet all my people,” he said. “But if I am called back to duty, I will go.”

title: The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
content:
The Pine Trees That Would Not Leave Me
While visiting the Lebanese mountain town Dhour El Choueir, I couldn't shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Six years ago, on August 4, 2020, a massive explosion at the Port of Beirut killed more than two hundred people, wounded thousands, and devastated large parts of the capital.
This August, sitting with a friend at a family-run restaurant amid the pine trees of Dhour El Choueir, a mountain town overlooking Beirut, I found myself unable to shake off a painting and a poem I had translated two decades earlier.
Lebanese painter Moustafa Farroukh’s watercolor “A Group of Pines in Bekfaya” was painted just a few miles from here in 1936. Born and first trained in Beirut under the painter Habib Serour, Farroukh later studied in Rome and Paris before returning to establish his practice in his native city. Through portraits and idealized landscapes, he offered a vivid vision of Lebanon’s people and terrain. Farroukh became a foundational figure in modern Lebanese painting, his art helping shape a visual language for the country while its political and cultural identity was still taking form under the French Mandate.
The painting of the pine grove was seared into my memory when I first saw it in 2003 in a catalog accompanying a Sursock Museum exhibition of Farroukh’s works. (The watercolor was on loan from the private collection of Emile Nasrallah.) Sursock itself later became a victim of the Beirut Port explosion. The blast shattered its stained-glass windows and damaged the historic building as well as dozens of artworks. The museum reopened on May 26, 2023, with five exhibitions, one of them titled Beyond Ruptures.
In August 1937, the Armenian poet Vahan Tekeyan was also here in Dhour El Choueir when he wrote the sonnet “To a Lebanese Pine Tree.”
I reconnected with the sonnet after returning home. I corrected a few errors in my translation, adjusted the wording and rhythms, and tried to bring the English closer to the movement of Tekeyan’s Armenian.
Here is the translation as I read it now, at twice the age I was when I first attempted it, with many more years of witnessing Lebanon from near and far.
To a Lebanese Pine Tree
By Vahan Tekeyan
Dhour El Choueir, Lebanon, August 1937
Your pain unfolds from the past, O soft-shadowed
pine tree… Barely risen from the ground
you have lost your maiden branch, the trace of which
appears on you, dried and jutting, like a severed arm.
Then countless others followed it, one after another…
Until, once they thought your trunk had grown large enough,
they let your upper branches sprout and thicken,
and slowly adorn themselves with translucent tresses.
And upon them too, how many fresh traces of the saw —
all your grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon,
whose open grave you have become beneath the skies…
But you do not at all inspire, O green tree of the mountains,
with memories of so many victims, any thought of mourning;
you ever bring forth new life and sway in joyous mood…
Born in Constantinople in 1878, Tekeyan came of age in an Armenian literary world that would be shattered during his lifetime. Poet, editor, teacher, and public figure, he belonged to a generation whose intellectual and literary lives cannot be separated from the violence that dispersed Ottoman Armenians across new geographies.
By 1937, Lebanon had become one of the epicenters of Armenian revival in the Middle East. Survivors of the Armenian Genocide had reconstituted community life away from their ancestral towns, rebuilding around churches and secular institutions.
Tekeyan participated directly in this process of revival. In September 1937, he became the first editor of a new Armenian newspaper in Beirut, Zartonk (“Awakening,” still published today). Tekeyan included “To a Lebanese Pine Tree,” written the previous month in Dhour El Choueir, in the paper’s inaugural issue, nestled among news items ranging from the upcoming parliamentary elections in French Mandate Lebanon and domestic politics in Palestine to the Spanish Civil War and Mussolini’s visit to Germany.
For all the Armenian resonances of Tekeyan’s wounded tree, the poem is emphatically Lebanese. Reading it in Lebanon in August 2026, I was struck less by what the pine might stand for than by how closely its contradictions seemed to belong to the country around me.
The poem begins with history lodged in the body. “Your pain unfolds from the past,” Tekeyan tells the tree.
The first wound appears low on the trunk. The lost branch resembles a human limb, its trace “dried and jutting, like a severed arm.” Before long, the instrument of amputation appears explicitly: the saw.
The mutilations accumulate. “Then countless others followed it, one after another.” Yet the tree continues upward. Its higher branches are eventually allowed to sprout and thicken, adorning themselves with “translucent tresses.” Tekeyan lets us glimpse flourishing before making us look again: those branches, too, bear “fresh traces of the saw.”
And then Tekeyan shifts the metaphor. The injured body becomes a genealogy. Its branches are its “grandchildren and great-grandchildren, dead too soon.” The ancestor remains standing as its descendants disappear around it.
Tekeyan then reverses the natural order of generations: The ancestor becomes the grave of its descendants, “whose open grave you have become beneath the skies.”
Everything in the sonnet seems to carry us toward grief.
Until it doesn’t.
“But you do not at all inspire,” Tekeyan writes, “any thought of mourning.”
And he tells us why: “You ever bring forth new life.”
In writing and conversation about Lebanon, the word “resilience” is tossed around liberally. But endlessly celebrating people’s resilience can normalize what they are repeatedly forced to endure.
No less common in Western media is the portrayal of Lebanon as hedonistic: its nightlife and crowded beach clubs, where the party continues amid economic collapse and political crisis. For decades, such coverage has treated the revival of Beirut’s bars and clubs as evidence that the country is “back.”
It is a seductive shorthand. But like the celebration of resilience, this framing romanticizes precarity and escapism while obscuring the scars of war and the uneven costs of crisis.
Tekeyan’s pine offers us something more compelling. Farroukh’s pines, in turn, offer a key to reading the poem.
Farroukh’s trees stand together.
Seen in this light, what is often flattened into hedonism may instead be understood as one manifestation of solidarity: an insistence on gathering with friends and family against the odds, even while bearing the traces of violence.
My grandparents were child survivors of the Armenian Genocide who found refuge in Lebanon, where my parents and I were born. I grew up during the Lebanese Civil War and came of age in its aftermath. When I first translated Tekeyan’s poem in 2003 and encountered Farroukh’s painting in the exhibition catalog that same year, I was still living there. Three years later came another war. Soon thereafter, I moved to the United States.
But it was only in Dhour El Choueir, in August 2026, that the poem and the painting came together for me, revealing something about Lebanon beyond the familiar scripts.
The wounds remain. The tree sways.
Acknowledgment: The author would like to thank Rowina Bou Harb, Head of Archives at the Sursock Museum, for her assistance.

title: 13 young people sued Hawaii over climate change. Here's what happened next
content:
Young people in Hawaii now meet regularly with the state’s Department of Transportation to offer input on public transit, bike lanes, and other strategies to help the department transition away from fossil fuels.
Establishing the Hawai‘i Youth Transportation Council was just one of the outcomes of the landmark 2024 settlement of the Navahine v. Hawai‘i DOT lawsuit, which was brought by 13 young plaintiffs.
Their lawsuit alleged that the DOT wasn’t making progress toward the climate goals set by the state, violating the plaintiffs’ constitutional right to a clean and healthful environment.
They settled the lawsuit in 2024 before it went to trial, and the DOT is now required to decarbonize transportation by 2045 and, through the youth council, to listen and incorporate the priorities of young Hawaiians.
Yale Climate Connections spoke with Charlotte Madin, one of the plaintiffs, and with Joanna Zeigler, a staff attorney at Our Children’s Trust who led the case.
This interview has been edited and shortened for clarity.
The impact of Navahine v. Hawai‘i DOT
Yale Climate Connections: Charlotte, what got you concerned about climate change in the first place?
Charlotte Madin: I was born in Sydney, Australia, and I lived there until I was eight years old. And while I lived there, my family and I would often experience really large heat waves that would make us essentially have to evacuate our home and go to the nearest air-conditioned place because my mother was concerned that my sister and I would be sick or have health concerns due to this heat.
The entire time I’ve lived in Hawaii, about eight years now, I’ve noticed the beautiful ocean and the biodiversity of the coral reefs just slowly becoming less and less healthy, which is really challenging to see, especially since both my parents are marine biologists.
So seeing that happen in real time in front of me was really scary. And then, in 2021, I was on the Big Island when there was a really large fire. There was ash raining from the sky. My grandmother had a concussion and couldn’t get to the hospital because the fire was blocking a route.
YCC: What inspired you to get involved in the lawsuit and to become a plaintiff?
Madin: When I was 12 years old, I did a short presentation for my community organization with a friend, and soon afterward she mentioned a lawsuit that she was joining that she told me would help us have a cleaner and healthier environment. Then later, her mom reached out and asked my mom, “Does your daughter want to join?” And I was like, “Yeah, if there’s a chance to help the environment while I’m still young, getting started early, I’ll take it.”
I had always been interested in climate change and in environmentalism and how we can sustain our climate for as long as possible, if not forever. And this just seemed like a really great jumping-off point for me.
YCC: Can you tell me a little bit about what it was like being a plaintiff?
Madin: I wasn’t really sure what was going to be expected of me when I joined the case. But over time it became clear that it was really helpful for me to appear at events surrounding our case to muster support from the community.
As for the actual legal dealings, I was deposed by lawyers from the Hawai’i Department of Transportation when I was 13 or 14, which was quite an experience. It was a lot of questions for three or four hours. And so that was probably one of the most defining moments of my career as a plaintiff in this case.
YCC: That must have been very intimidating. What was that like, and what did you do to prepare for that?
Madin: Yeah, it was very intimidating. I remember being really, really nervous for the days leading up to the deposition. But I was told to tell the truth — you know, they won’t be able to find anything wrong with that, take it slow, take a deep breath if you need to, and don’t feel pressured to answer anything.
And that advice served me well throughout the deposition. By the end of it, I was exhausted, but I was really happy and proud of what I accomplished and what I’d done.
YCC: Can either of you give me a little bit of an overview of what the lawsuit alleged?
Joanna Zeigler: There were two constitutional provisions that were brought in the lawsuit. The first one is the public trust doctrine, which provides that the state shall conserve and protect Hawaii’s natural beauty and all of its natural resources for the benefit of present and future generations.
The second constitutional provision brought in the case was the right to a clean and healthful environment. And that gives each person the right to a clean and healthful environment as defined by the Hawaii statutes.
YCC: How much was the Department of Transportation relying on fossil fuels when this began? And can you put that in the context of any carbon reduction goals or mandates that had already been set prior to this?
Zeigler: The transportation sector is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Hawaii, and transportation emissions are projected to continue to rise. Historically, HDOT’s planning of ground transportation has been very car-centric, prioritizing projects such as road expansion and maintenance rather than projects that reduce greenhouse gas emissions, such as pedestrian, bicycle, and transit expansion and expansion of EV infrastructure.
So without breaking that “business-as-usual” planning process of planning for more and more cars on the road, emissions from transportation would continue to be a problem.
YCC: What are some of the major points that the settlement requires the government to do?
Zeigler: The settlement requires HDOT to decarbonize the transportation sector by 2045, which means zero emissions from ground, marine, and inter-island air transportation. And the settlement provides benchmarks and requirements for what HDOT needs to do to reach zero emissions.
So for example, HDOT agreed to draft a greenhouse gas reduction plan, which is its road map to how it will reach zero emissions by 2045, with benchmarks for 2030, 2035, and 2040. HDOT also agreed to complete the pedestrian, bicycle, and transit network within five years of when the settlement was reached and increase EV infrastructure.
And so this settlement is a complement to the state laws which require statewide net-negative emissions by 2045 and require HDOT to decarbonize the transportation sector. But now we have this enforceable contract to help hold HDOT accountable for its part in decarbonizing the transportation sector. So the youth are in a contract with HDOT, and HDOT has made these promises to the youth to decarbonize.
And one other aspect of the settlement is that HDOT created the youth council. It’s an opportunity for youth from across Hawaii to provide feedback and let HDOT know what their priorities are so that HDOT can take those into consideration when it’s planning and prioritizing projects.
So there are so many aspects of the settlement that are really exciting, and watching it unfold has been a tremendous accomplishment.
YCC: What is the significance of this particular case?
Zeigler: This is the first youth-led climate change case to have reached a settlement agreement, and HDOT came to an agreement that will have a tremendous impact on the youth’s future and the future of Hawaii.
This is an example of what can be accomplished when government works with the youth, rather than against them, by sitting down at the table and truly listening to why the youth brought the case and what they were hoping to accomplish.
So with the settlement, HDOT has a backstop to the policies and practices that it puts in place, and the legislature also has a role to play to make sure that the state policies are in place to promote decarbonizing transportation so that HDOT can fulfill its agreement.
Other states can look to the progress that Hawaii is making and how it is improving the lives of its citizens and hopefully use Hawaii as a model for what can be accomplished with government cooperation.
YCC: Are youth lawsuits an effective approach to climate action and to holding some of these entities accountable?
Zeigler: Courts have a role to play in climate justice because the courts are there to ensure that the legislative and executive branches are acting within the confines of state statutes, or as in our cases, within the confines of the state or United States Constitution.
So in our system of checks and balances, the court must interpret the Constitution and make sure that the actions of the state are not violating these youths’ fundamental rights, which include the right to live in a world with a stable climate system.
YCC: Charlotte, what are some of the parts of the plan that you’re most excited about and some of the priorities that you want to make sure are seen through throughout this process?
Madin: I love the youth council aspect of the plan, and it’s been super exciting because I get to meet all these incredible young people from all around Hawaii and to hear their ideas and what they hope for, and to also be able to have this voice in not only the Hawaii Department of Transportation’s planning, but also, because of this, being given an intro into legislation and how bills work.
YCC: Is there anything else that either of you wanted to add to help people understand about this?
Madin: Well, I guess a message for the young people out there: You always have a voice, and you always have a choice with how you use that. And utilizing the power of democracy and utilizing the legal system, you can do big things with your voice.
So never give up your voice, and don’t let others silence you. Just do what you believe, and everything will work out fine in the end.
This article was originally published by Yale Climate Connections.

title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
content:
The steel 'embodies his soul': 9/11 family takes World Trade Center beam across US
Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11.
On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner.
"He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News.
"When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan."
He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center.
Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old.
Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired.
The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News.
9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live.
Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful."
At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago."
To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's.
"Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across."
The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many."
As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11.
"And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot."
"Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel."
Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks.
"We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain.
Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said.
As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled.
"Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said.
"I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said.
To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign.
"These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids."
"I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made."
The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes.
"We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said.
"Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

title: 6,000 People, 27 Villages & One Zero-Waste Mission
content: In Zemithang, Arunachal Pradesh, communities come together every Sunday to keep their Himalayan home clean. Residents wash, dry and sort their waste into 22 categories, including plastic, glass and metal. Every household contributes ₹50, while women riders collect the segregated waste and take it to a recycling centre. Started by Merwyn Coutinho in 2020, the Himalayan Fringes Project has impacted 20,000+ people and recovered nearly 90 tonnes of waste. No fancy technology. title: Group to showcase Domboshava heritage at Bira reMbira
content:
Herald Reporter
DOMBOSHAVA’S Mbira Dzepadombo Ensemble will be among featured groups at this year’s Bira reMbira National Festival, bringing the area’s rich mbira traditions to the national cultural showcase at the Glamis Arena on Friday.
The third edition of Bira reMbira, which starts at 10am on September 25 and runs through to the morning of September 26, will bring together leading “gwenyambiras” master mbira players in a celebration of traditional acoustic music, spiritual heritage and the country’s mbira value chain.
The festival is being held under the theme “Roots to Markets – Empowering Makers, Players and Markets”, according to the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture’s official festival brief.
The festival is being held with support from the Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture and the Ministry of Tourism and Hospitality Industry.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the festival provides an important national platform to showcase the cultural traditions of Domboshava while highlighting ongoing efforts to preserve and pass on mbira knowledge to younger generations.
The ensemble was initiated by Dr Pearson Pfavayi, a tourism and cultural heritage advocate who recognised the deep cultural and spiritual connection between mbira music and the Domboshava community.
The group has been selected as one of the featured ensembles at Bira reMbira 2026 in recognition of its artistry, cultural preservation work and performance standards.
It will be led by master “gwenyambira,” Sekuru Thomas Chiombera, alongside Percy Dandiro, David Matiza and Nokutenda Kadzima.
Dr Pfavayi said the group’s participation was part of a broader effort to ensure that mbira remains a living cultural tradition rather than merely a historical artefact.
“Mbira is a sacred art form and a foundational pillar of our Zimbabwean cultural heritage that we must actively honour, preserve and identify with. Through Mbira Dzepadombo, we seek to safeguard these ancient rhythms while creating opportunities for people to learn, experience and appreciate their cultural significance,” he said.
The group’s activities are closely linked to Basecamp Domboshava, which serves as the home of Mbira Dzepadombo.
Situated at the foot of the historic Domboshava Caves and granite mountain, Basecamp Domboshava brings together cultural heritage preservation, community arts and adventure tourism.
A Mbira Training Centre is set to commence training on October 10, offering structured lessons to local youths, national students and international visitors in traditional mbira tuning, crafting and playing techniques.
The training centre forms part of the broader cultural activities being developed at Basecamp Domboshava, which also operates alongside Domboview Adventures, providing a base for guided cave hikes, team-building activities, art gallery sales and traditional food experiences.
Dr Pfavayi said the forthcoming training programme would help strengthen the inter-generational transmission of mbira knowledge.
“By establishing Mbira Dzepadombo and our dedicated Mbira Training Centre at Basecamp Domboshava, our mission is to preserve traditional knowledge and skills while opening the mbira experience to young Zimbabweans, visitors and international audiences,” he said.
The 2026 Bira reMbira festival will feature a wide range of artistes and mbira groups, including Victor Kunonga, Feli Nandi, Andy Muridzo, Duramazwi, Nyamasvisva Nemaungira Enharira, Amadhuve, Sasha, Kurai Makore, Mangwenya, Diana Samkange, Vee Mhofu, Texas Tekenya, Jah Lemmy, Gushungo, Jaka Band, Lioness Shumbakadzi, Ntswai Ntswai Arts, Brity Yonly, NzombeHuru Mbira Ensemble, Pauline Mafriq, Tatu Maluba, Dzambira, Mbira Dzenharo, Ambuya Mavhu Mbira Group, Chikwata 263, Batroy Movement, Nemachinda Ehondo Crew, Nina X and Zariyah Roots Band, Professor Muzvinafundo, Sekuru Gore and Mazana Movement, Ruyamuro Mbira Crew, Rose Wembira, Madzimambo Edu Mbira Family, Culture Livingstone, Dzimbanwe Mbira Crew, Pastoral Entertainment Group, Masimba Evanhu Mbira Group, Madzinza Embira, Dzamawuruka Mbira Band, Sekuru Mushore Mbira Custodians, Chishawasha Nhare Mbira Group, Izwi Remhondoro Mbira Group, Mbira Dzepadombo, Jangu Wiriranai Arts and Mbira Group and Nelson Tswatswa.
The extensive line-up reflects the organisers’ intention to bring together established musicians, emerging performers and traditional mbira ensembles under one platform.
Festival organiser Benjamin “Benjie” Nyandoro said Bira reMbira was designed to create a meeting point for musicians, cultural practitioners, audiences and the wider creative economy.
“Bira reMbira is more than a music event. It is a platform for Zimbabweans to celebrate their heritage while creating opportunities for musicians, instrument makers, cultural practitioners and young creatives. Our intention is to connect the roots of mbira with markets so that those who preserve and promote this heritage can also find sustainable opportunities within the creative economy,” he said.
The festival will provide a free-to-the-public cultural experience and will feature established and emerging mbira musicians, school ensembles and young creative collectives.
There will also be exhibitions showcasing mbira instruments, national fabric, herbs and medicinal plants, indigenous foods and other expressions of Zimbabwe’s diverse cultural heritage.
A major feature of this year’s festival will be a special tribute honouring the late Mbuya Stella Chiweshe, one of Zimbabwe’s foremost mbira practitioners and cultural ambassadors.
The Ministry’s official brief states that the festival will honour her through dedicated performances of her songs in a commemorative segment highlighting her influence on contemporary mbira practice.
Her artistic journey, leadership and longstanding commitment to the mbira tradition inspired generations of musicians, cultural practitioners and mbira custodians.
The tribute will form part of a broader celebration of Zimbabwe’s living heritage, with performers using the festival to demonstrate how the mbira continues to evolve while remaining rooted in traditional practice.
For Mbira Dzepadombo, the Bira reMbira appearance will be followed by another community-focused engagement when the ensemble is scheduled to perform at the Pinktober Breast Cancer Awareness Event on October 31.
The performance will form part of activities supporting cancer survivors and breast cancer awareness.
The continued involvement of Mbira Dzepadombo in cultural, tourism and community initiatives reflects the group’s broader objective of using mbira as a vehicle for cultural education, heritage preservation and community engagement.
The Ministry of Sport, Recreation, Arts and Culture has said Bira reMbira complements the Government’s broader cultural development agenda by creating platforms for heritage preservation, youth participation, creative enterprise, skills development, market access and cultural diplomacy.
As Glamis Arena prepares to host the overnight cultural gathering, Mbira Dzepadombo will carry with it the sounds and traditions of Domboshava, giving audiences an opportunity to experience a living heritage that continues to evolve while remaining rooted in Zimbabwean cultural identity.
